title: Cornell alleged gang rape: New documents detail timeline before Jane Doe spoke to police, NYT reports | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

In the three weeks between when a former Cornell University student wasallegedly gang rapedat a fraternity house to her describing the night to campus police, Jane Doe appeared to grapple with shame and her stance had evolved on whether an assault took place, according to theNew York Timesciting records it exclusively obtained of the university’s investigation at the time.

In an article published Thursday, the Times cited documents from the university’s formal Title IX investigation that shed new light on how Doe initially viewed the night’s events, discussing it with her roommates and communicating with some of the men, before she reported the alleged sexual assault to university police.

The revelations come after details emerged this week from Doe’s signed police statement, in which she recounted being hit and feeling emotionally coerced into sexual activity while intoxicated.

She also made a more explicit accusation of rape in a November 2024 interview with campus police – the transcript of which Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten told CNNhis office never receivedbefore deciding not to bring charges in the case that has nowsparked national outrage.

CNN has reached out to Van Houten on whether his office received the findings from the Title IX investigation. CNN has not seen the Title IX filings, which are generally confidential and restricted to the parties involved.

In a response to CNN, Doe’s attorney, Thomas P. Giuffra, said the latest findings from the Times detail how “Doe’s internal processing went from denial, to shame and ultimately acceptance that she had been raped by people that she thought were her friends. Her reactions were a textbook reaction to trauma.”

Cornell hassaidpolice followed protocol and shared “all investigatory information” with the DA, as questions swirl surrounding the initial investigation and what the county district attorney knew about the allegations. Here’s what we know.

Included in the documents compiled during the university investigation were hundreds of pages of emails, text messages, photographs and interviews with Doe, her friends and six of the seven men she accused, according to the Times. The files also included an extensive transcript of the original police interviews with the woman, the outlet reported.

After the alleged gang rape at Chi Phi fraternity that began on October 19, 2024, Doe recounted the night’s events to her roommates without identifying herself as a rape victim, the Times reports citing the files.

The following narrative comes from the Times’ review of the Title IX files it obtained.

Doe reportedly told her two roommates the day she returned home that she had consumed ketamine and had sex with multiple men. One roommate told investigators that Jane Doe did not use the word “rape” or “assault” yet.

One roommate said she could not remember Doe saying yes to anything that occurred while another roommate said it appeared Doe was “in shock,” the roommate told investigators, “not really understanding the gravity of what she was saying.”

The next day, Doe reportedly spoke with her sorority big sister, who later told investigators “what she was going through is that she had not yet processed what had happened.”

Doe had also been in communication with at least two of the men she later accused of sexual assault, according to the Times.

One reportedly sent Doe a text message, which said: “I just wanted to apologize for how things went down the other night,” adding he and another of the men allegedly involved felt terrible and too under the influence of drugs and alcohol to “shut it down and kick people out before it got way out of hand.”

She replied to the man reassuringly, the Times reported, saying “non of the sexual stuff was illegal.”

On Oct. 22, Doe saw a Cornell Health doctor because she had contracted a urinary tract infection and wanted to be tested for sexually transmitted diseases, the Times said citing the documents. She told the doctor she contracted the UTI “in a traumatic way,” according to a transcript of her conversation with investigators. Doe said the doctor suggested she go to therapy.

In a statement to CNN, Doe’s attorney said his office was not aware whether the findings of the Title IX investigation were shared with Cornell police, but said the information “would have significant probative value in a criminal investigation.”

“I believe that the information was not (shared with police), because what is contained in the proceedings is evidence of several crimes being committed with excellent supporting evidence,” Giuffra told CNN, adding Title IX proceedings and access to these documents are limited to school officials, involved parties and their lawyers.

When Doe first visited a university health clinic, she was not referred any resources available for survivors of sexual assault, Giuffra added, stressing that the disclosure “warranted further inquiry, including a rape kit, consultation of medical professionals trained to deal with rape cases and a physical exam to document her injuries.”

In the weeks after the alleged gang rape, interviews with Doe, her roommates and her sorority big sister describe a 20-year-old sophomore girl realizing the severity of the event’s nights and understanding the events as an alleged assault, according to the Times.

The documents reportedly detail how rumors about the alleged gang rape led her to fear reputational damage and left her humiliated.

It was an evolution of thought complicated by Doe’s history as a sexual assault survivor, the Times reports, citing the documents. In the six-page summary signed by Doe to police, she described having a prior “traumatic experience” regarding sexual intercourse.

After the alleged rape, Doe saw comments on an online forum about Greek life on Chi Phi brothers drugging and gang raping a sophomore, which she later told investigators, according to the Times: “That’s the first time I had ever heard the narrative change that I wasn’t a whore and that I was assaulted.”

On Nov. 3, Doe texts one of the men, explicitly telling them that what happened on that October night was not consensual. According to the Times, she wrote: “let’s be clear that 90% of what happened that night was not consensual. i was given more key than i can remember,” using a shorthand for ketamine, “and i know that i told u i felt uncomfortable and i didn’t know anyone in the room.”

Before going to campus police, Doe reportedly collected evidence, including photos of the bruises on her body allegedly caused by one of the men hitting her. She also had not washed the dress to save as potential evidence, the Times reports.

On Nov. 7, Doe went to an emergency room in Ithaca, where Cornell is located, and requested a rape kit, the Times reports citing the documents.

In a 2024 statement to Cornell police, obtained by CNN from a source familiar with the investigation, Doe recounted arriving at the Chi Phi fraternity house and dancing with one person who asked if she would be interested in participating in a threesome, telling police she was “pretty ok” with aspects of an initial encounter, but that later in the night she did not consent to other sexual activities, according to the six-page statement.

“I felt like I was unable to make any decisions because of how intoxicated I was,” she said in the statement. Doe said she felt like her overall intoxication level at one point was about an “8 out of 10” — which she said was the most intoxicated she had been in her life.

She described being “pretty incapacitated,” feeling uncomfortable, swatting one man’s hand away several times and being “horrified” as more men entered the room they were in. She said she “finally gave in” to one later encounter after she was asked “to have sex so many times,” according to the statement.

“To me that felt like coercion,” she said in the statement. “Also, I felt like due to my intoxication, they should have known how intoxicated I was based on how I was slurring my words.”

Doe made a more explicit accusation of rape in a separate document, according toCNN affiliate WCBS. The station obtained a transcript of a November 2024 interview with campus police from a source.

“I can say with 100% confidence I was raped,” Doe said in the transcript, according to WCBS.

CNN has not seen the transcript and has asked Cornell for a copy but has not heard back. The transcript is a separate document from the six-page statement that was submitted by the university.

Beyond alleged emotional pressure, Doe told police in the statement she was physically hit and remembered feeling hurt. “One hit in particular sent a sharp pain through me,” she said. The student also described noticing bruising on her body the following day.

Doe also described she “had become extremely uncomfortable with how this night was turning out” and thought, “if I passed out and the men had sex with me, then they could be charged with Rape,” the statement reads.

Doe told police she remembered consuming a “heavy amount” of ketamine, smoking marijuana and having “various things” poured on her body. She said she initially agreed to having drugs consumed off her body while feeling “extremely tired” but “couldn’t tell what they were pouring on me.”

Doe reported the alleged incident to Cornell police on November 8, 2024, weeks after the alleged assault, according to a civilcomplaintfiled last month. In the days following the alleged incident, she was “traumatized, numb and unable to function or accept the horror of what had happened,” Doe’s attorney, Thomas P. Giuffra, told CNN.

Although Cornell said it provided the district attorney’s office with a police investigation report, Van Houten told CNN his office was not given the interview transcript before deciding no charges should be filed in the investigation.

Van Houten told CNN on Wednesday morning that the university had still not provided his office with the transcript. CNN had also reached out to Van Houten about whether it received the Title IX filings.

The DA said it was Doe’s six-page statement thatdetermined no chargesshould be filed, adding, “Multiple prosecutors and criminal investigators reviewed Jane Doe’s statement and correctly determined the alleged facts as set forth in the statement do not constitute a crime.”

Van Houten said he learned of the more explicit allegation made in the interview when he was contacted by WCBS on Tuesday evening and said his office will be investigating the reported statements “fully.”

When reached by CNN about the DA’s comments, a Cornell University spokesperson did not specifically address the transcript but said it “shared all investigatory information” with the DA’s office.

Cornell hasn’t responded to repeated requests to explain or clarify whether that turnover included the interview transcript.

The university likely did not break any laws if it did neglect to share all relevant documents with the DA, said former prosecutor Gary Galperin, while acknowledging that not sharing all documents would violate “all principles of what’s logical and decent.”

The DA’s comments Wednesday raised new questions about what law enforcement knew in the weeks after the alleged assault and why no criminal charges were filed.

“It is a case that, clearly, just on the face of her statement, is so complex and so nuanced,” former Westchester County DA Mimi Rocah told CNN’s Jake Tapper.

“If you’re an investigator trying to get at the truth, as this DA office should have been, they should have sought more information,” she added.

Van Houten canceled his appearance on CNN Wednesday evening, saying, “At this time I need to shift my focus to the investigation and to pursuing the additional evidence that has recently come to light.”

He said his office will keep the public informed of developments in the investigation and any action of the Tompkins County Grand Jury.

The unfolding details of Jane Doe’s case have sparked renewed attention to the ongoing topic of sexual assault awareness and prevention on college campuses.

Doe’s attorney has said Cornellexpelledtwo of the seven accused students while the others received lesser punishments, including suspensions, workshops or written assignments.

Cornell has countered that claim, saying “none of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement.”

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said Cornell has agreed to anoutside investigationto “determine whether Cornell met every obligation to protect its students and pursue justice,” she told CNN. The university confirmed that it agreed to the investigation and declined to provide further details.

The Chi Phi national fraternity said in a Wednesday statement that it condemns sexual assault and drug and alcohol abuse, and three days after Doe filed a police report, the fraternity chapter “voted unanimously to remove the accused members from its rolls” and “recommended that our national fraternity permanently expel them,” which it said the fraternity’s Grand Council did in a subsequent meeting.

“These actions went beyond anything the law or Cornell University required of us,” the fraternity added in the statement.

The school also said it hadclosedthat chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity in 2024, and that the chapter remains barred from campus.

It is unclear if any of the accused men are still Cornell students.

Lawmakers, current and former Cornell students, actors and other public figures are among those who have spoken out.

In another effort for future accountability, Ithaca Mayor Robert Cantelmo told CNN he has asked Cornell to consider an agreement to loop in the Ithaca Police Department whenever incidents involving sexual assault are reported on campus. Cantelmo said he was waiting for a response from the university.

Giuffra said it had been Doe’s dream to go to Cornell, which she no longer attends.

It’s unclear how extensive that initial police investigation was, but Doe’s attorney says he believes it was inadequate.

“It is challenging for me to understand how a thorough criminal investigation could have been conducted when she never spoke with anyone other than the officer who took her original complaint,” Giuffrasaid.

Help is available: For help in the US, call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at1-800-656-4673or chat 24/7 ononline.rainn.org.

CNN’s Danya Gainor, Jason Carroll, Gloria Pazmino, Chris Boyette, Cindy Von Quednow and Avni Trivedi contributed to this report.
